parts.problem_md: Define the term **limited liability**.

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> Most people recognise Heinz for the phrase ‘57 varieties’ even though it now produces many more than the original 57 varieties. H J Heinz, the founder of the Heinz business, believed the phrase sounded lucky.
> 
> *Kraft Heinz *is a world-wide producer of food products. It was formed from the merger of Kraft Foods and Heinz in 2015. This created the third largest food and drinks business in the USA and the fifth largest food and drinks business in the world.
> 
> *Kraft Heinz* has over 24 different brands, including Greenseas in Australia and Nutri+Plus in New Zealand. America has the largest number of brands from Maxwell House to Cool Whip. *Kraft Heinz* produces many different products including tomato sauce, ‘Mac&Cheese’, pasta and its famous baked beans that are used and eaten by many people.
> 
> *Kraft Heinz* uses many methods to advertise its products. These include posters, billboards and leaflets in supermarkets.
> 
> On 13 September 2022 the share price of Kraft Heinz in America at 10.00 am was \$36.55 and at 4.00 pm it was \$35.06.

Which **one** of the following is the percentage decrease in the share price?

Select **one** answer
parts.solution_md:
**The correct answer is C** — 4.08%

The percentage decrease is calculated as:

`equals space fraction numerator 36.55 minus 35.06 over denominator 36.55 end fraction space cross times space 100

equals fraction numerator 1.49 over denominator 36.55 end fraction space cross times space 100

equals 4.08 percent sign`

**A** is incorrect as 1.49 is simply the difference between $36 . 55 - 35 . 06$, not expressed as a percentage

**B** is incorrect as 1.96 results from dividing the sum of the two prices by 36.55 rather than the difference

**D** is incorrect as 4.25 results from dividing the difference by the closing price rather than the opening price:

`equals space fraction numerator 1.49 over denominator 35.06 end fraction space cross times space 100

equals 4.25 percent sign`

parts.problem_md: Explain **one** advantage to a business of having limited liability.
parts.solution_md:
The business exists as a separate legal entity to its owners **[1 mark]. **If the business goes into debt **[1 mark] **the business owners are protected from losing their personal assets **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Award 1 mark for identifying an advantage to a business of having limited liability
> 
> 2 further marks are awarded for explaining the advantage, for a maximum of 3 marks
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer**
> 
> - The business may raise large amounts of finance to expand **[1 mark] **through selling shares **[1 mark] a**s investors only risk losing the value of their shares if the business fails **[1 mark]**
> - Accept any other appropriate response
> 
> Answers that list three advantages to a business of having limited liability with no explanation will get a maximum of 1 mark
> 
> No marks are awarded for a definition alone

> **[exam-tip]**
> Make sure you develop your answer fully rather than simply listing multiple advantages. The question asks you to explain **one** advantage, so pick one and expand on it in a chain of reasoning (point → cause/effect → consequence for the business). A common mistake is writing a definition of limited liability without linking it to an advantage — this will not earn any marks. Aim to write three connected sentences that build logically on each other to secure all 3 marks.

**[3 marks]**

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> *IKEA* is a well-known home furniture retailer with stores throughout the world. It was started in 1943 by Ingvar Kamprad when he was given some money by his father for doing well at school. He wanted to produce furniture at a price that people could afford to buy.
> 
> He realised that transporting furniture to customers was difficult as goods were often damaged. He developed flat packs to avoid damage. A flat pack contained all the materials needed to self-assemble a table, a chair or a bed.
> 
> All *IKEA* stores are run as franchises.

Analyse the benefits to* IKEA* of all its stores being franchises
parts.solution_md:
Franchisees will have local knowledge of the market in their country **[1 mark]**. This helps IKEA to offer products that suit local customers' tastes and needs **[1 mark]**, which could lead to higher sales of its affordable flat-pack furniture **[1 mark]**

Additionally, IKEA's brand and reputation are maintained by franchisees **[1 mark] **who follow its established business model. This means IKEA can ensure a consistent customer experience across its stores worldwide **[1 mark]**, helping to build customer loyalty and repeat purchases **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Award up to 2 marks for identifying benefits to IKEA of all its stores being franchises
> 
> Up to 2 further marks are awarded for applying the benefits to IKEA's context
> 
> Up to 2 further marks are awarded for explaining the benefits to the business
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer**
> 
> - Franchisees pay IKEA a fee to operate under its brand name **[1 mark]**. This provides IKEA with a regular stream of income that can be used to invest in developing new products **[1 mark]**, such as improving its flat-pack furniture range **[1 mark]**
> - Franchisees are also responsible for the day-to-day running and costs of their own stores **[1 mark]**. This means IKEA can expand into new countries without taking on the financial risk itself **[1 mark]**, allowing it to grow quickly while keeping its own costs low **[1 mark]**
> - Accept any other appropriate response
> 
> Answers that list six benefits to IKEA of all its stores being franchises with no explanation will get a maximum of 1 mark
> 
> No marks are awarded for a definition alone

> **[exam-tip]**
> When a question asks you to "analyse", you need to do more than just state facts. Make sure you apply your knowledge to the specific business in the extract — in this case, IKEA and its flat pack furniture — and then develop your points by explaining the consequences or impact on the business. A good approach is to make a point, link it to the extract, and then explain why it matters for IKEA. For example, don't just say "franchisees pay fees" — go on to explain what this means for IKEA's revenue and success. Aim to write at least two or three well-developed points to access the full range of marks across both AO2 and AO3.

**[6 marks]**

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> BrightSpark is an electrical repair business in Manchester, England. It was set up two years ago by two friends, Amir and Priya, who each invested £5,000 of their own savings. The business has grown quickly and now employs four technicians. Amir and Priya currently operate as a partnership but are considering becoming a private limited company.

Analyse the benefits to BrightSpark of becoming a private limited company.
parts.solution_md:
A private limited company has a separate legal identity from its owners **[1 mark]**, meaning BrightSpark would continue to exist even if Amir or Priya decided to leave **[1 mark]**. This gives the business greater stability and permanence, which could help build trust with customers and suppliers as BrightSpark continues to grow **[1 mark]**

Becoming a private limited company could also make BrightSpark appear more professional and credible **[1 mark]**. Customers in Manchester may feel more confident using an established company for electrical repairs rather than a partnership **[1 mark]**, which could help attract more business and allow BrightSpark to compete with larger, more established competitors **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Award up to 2 marks for identifying benefits to BrightSpark of becoming a private limited company
> 
> Up to 2 further marks are awarded for applying the benefits to BrightSpark's context
> 
> Up to 2 further marks are awarded for explaining the benefits to the business
> 
> **Alternative ways to answer**
> 
> - As a partnership, Amir and Priya have unlimited liability, meaning their personal belongings could be used to pay off business debts **[1 mark]**. Becoming a private limited company would remove this risk, which is especially important now that BrightSpark employs four technicians and has greater financial commitments such as wages **[1 mark]**, making the consequences of failure much higher **[1 mark]**

This could help Amir and Priya to define their individual roles and responsibilities more effectively as the business grows **[1 mark]**, reducing the chance of disagreements and ensuring BrightSpark is run more efficiently **[1 mark]**

> **[case-study]**
> The Alternative Drum School (TADS) was set up in the wealthy area of Cricklade, England in 2008 by Ollie Tanner who had a passion for and enjoyed drumming. Ollie invested all of his savings into the drumming school. He saw the potential of being located away from other drumming schools.
> 
> Ollie promotes his business by writing columns in local papers, performing at local music festivals and by word of mouth recommendations. He has invested heavily in computer technology to allow students to produce the music they enjoy playing.
> 
> Ollie finds it difficult to maintain a good work-life balance. Ollie currently works 60 hours a week in a business that does not have reliable profits.
> 
> At the moment *TADS* operates as a sole trader. As it becomes more successful Ollie is considering becoming a private limited company.

Evaluate whether *TADS* should consider becoming a private limited company. You should use the information provided as well as your own knowledge of business.
parts.solution_md:
A private limited company is a business where ownership is divided into shares that can be sold privately to family, friends or investors, but not to the general public **[K]**

Becoming a private limited company would give Ollie the benefit of limited liability **[K]**. This means that if TADS fails, Ollie can only lose the money he has invested in the business, and his personal assets would be protected **[An]**. This is important because Ollie has already invested all of his savings into TADS **[Ap]**, and the business does not have reliable profits **[Ap]**, so there is a real risk he could lose everything if things go wrong. As a sole trader, Ollie has unlimited liability, which puts him in a very vulnerable position **[An]**. Also, by selling shares to investors, Ollie could raise additional finance  **[K] **to grow the business further, such as investing in more computer technology **[Ap]**

However, becoming a private limited company means Ollie would have to share ownership and decision-making with other shareholders **[K]**, which means he could lose some control over how TADS is run **[An]**. Since Ollie set up the business because of his passion for drumming **[Ap]**, having others influence decisions may take the business in a direction he does not want **[An]**. Setting up a private limited company also involves legal costs and paperwork **[K]**, which could be difficult for a small business with unreliable profits  **[Ap]** **[An]**

Overall, TADS should become a private limited company **[E]**. Remaining as a sole trader leaves Ollie exposed to unlimited liability, meaning he could lose his personal possessions if the business fails. He is also working 60 hours a week with unreliable profits **[Ap] **and no way to bring in extra finance, which is not sustainable **[E]**. While becoming a private limited company means sharing some control, Ollie could keep a majority of the shares to protect his vision for TADS while gaining limited liability and access to new investment that could help stabilise and grow the business **[E]**

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> Smile Dental Practice is a small dental clinic in Lisbon, Portugal. It was set up two years ago by Dr Amara Osei as a sole trader. The business has grown steadily thanks to positive online reviews and word-of-mouth recommendations from satisfied patients. It now has a waiting list of over 50 patients. Amara is struggling to manage the workload alone and often works late into the evening, which is affecting her work-life balance. She wants to bring in another dentist to help the business grow.

Amara is considering two options for changing the structure of the business:

- Option 1: Form a partnership with another qualified dentist
- Option 2: Establish a private limited company and sell shares to raise finance for expansion

Justify which one of these two options Smile Dental Practice should choose.
parts.solution_md:
A partnership is a business owned by two or more people who share responsibility for running the business **[K]**. A private limited company is a business whose shares can be sold privately to raise finance and whose owners benefit from limited liability **[K]**

Forming a partnership with another dentist would allow Amara to share the workload **[K]** immediately. This would help reduce her long working hours **[Ap] **and improve her work-life balance while also allowing Smile to see more of the 50 patients currently on the waiting list, increasing revenue **[An]**

However, in a partnership, Amara would have to share the profits **[K]** with the new dentist **[Ap]**. She would also still have unlimited liability **[K]**, meaning her personal assets could be at risk if the business ran into debt. Additionally, Amara and her partner may disagree on how to run the practice, which could slow down decision-making **[An]**

Establishing a private limited company would give Amara limited liability, protecting her personal assets if the business were to fail **[K]**. Selling shares could also raise enough finance to hire additional staff, buy new equipment and expand the clinic **[Ap]**, allowing Smile to grow beyond what a simple partnership could achieve **[An]**

The drawback is that setting up a private limited company involves legal costs and paperwork **[K]**, which takes time and money. Amara would also have to share ownership with shareholders, and the process of establishing the company would not immediately solve her workload problem or reduce the waiting list **[Ap] [An]**

Smile should choose Option 1 **[E]**. Amara's most urgent problem is her heavy workload and poor work-life balance **[Ap]**, and a partnership would solve this straight away by bringing in another qualified dentist **[E]**. Becoming a private limited company would take time to set up and would not directly address the immediate need for another dentist to help with the growing patient waiting list **[E]**

> 
> **Alternative ways to answer**
> 
> - A new partner could bring specialist dental skills that Amara does not have → allow Smile to offer a wider range of treatments → attracting new patients and increasing revenue
> - Finding the right partner is risky → if the new dentist does not match Amara's standards, it could lead to poor patient experiences → damaging the strong reputation Smile has built through positive reviews over the past two years

> **[case-study]**
> Pulse is a small chain of three fitness studios based in Tenerife, Spain. It was founded in 2018 by Elena Vargas, a former personal trainer, who used her savings and a bank loan to set up the business. Pulse offers high-intensity group classes and personal training sessions using a unique training method that Elena developed herself. The studios have become popular through social media and positive customer reviews, and Elena has built up €120,000 in retained profit over the past three years.
> 
> Elena personally trains all new instructors to make sure they deliver classes to her standard. She believes the quality of instruction is what sets Pulse apart from other gyms in Tenerife. Each studio is designed with the same layout, colour scheme and branding.
> 
> Elena wants to expand Pulse across mainland Spain and into other European countries. However, opening new studios requires significant investment in equipment, premises and staff training. Elena is considering whether to sell franchises as a way to grow the business.

Evaluate whether Pulse should sell franchises to expand the business. You should use the information provided as well as your own knowledge of business.
parts.solution_md:
A franchise is where a business allows another operator to trade under its name in exchange for a fee **[K]**

Selling franchises would allow Pulse to expand across mainland Spain and into Europe without Elena having to fund each new studio herself **[K]**. Franchisees would pay for their own premises, equipment and staff, meaning Pulse can grow quickly while Elena keeps her €120,000 in retained profit **[Ap] **as a financial safety net rather than spending it all on expansion **[An]**

However, Elena currently trains all new instructors personally to maintain quality, which is what she believes sets Pulse apart **[Ap]**. If franchisees are responsible for running their own studios, Elena may not be able to oversee training at every location **[K]**. This could lead to inconsistent quality of instruction, which might damage the reputation that Pulse has built through positive reviews and social media **[An]**

Overall, Pulse should not sell franchises at this stage **[E]**. Elena's hands-on approach to training and her unique method  **[Ap] **are the core reasons for the business's success, and these would be very difficult to maintain across multiple franchise locations in different countries **[E]**. Instead, Elena could use her retained profit to open one or two new studios herself on the mainland, keeping full control over the quality of instruction and the consistent branding  **[Ap] **that makes Pulse distinctive **[E]**. Franchising could be reconsidered in the future once Pulse has established a proven system for training instructors without Elena's direct involvement **[E]**
